title: Paid per weed, garden ignored
allegory: Reward hacking is like paying a child a coin per weed pulled to get a tidy garden: they find the one patch that regrows overnight and pull it every morning, collecting plenty of coins while the rest of the garden runs wild, because you paid for pulling, not for tidiness.
map: the outcome you meant: the true objective
the reward you wrote down: a proxy for that objective
a loophole where the proxy is high and the goal isn't, like CoastRunners' respawning targets
a child who only counts coins, and gets better at it
the optimiser: more pressure finds the gap between proxy and goal more reliably
watching rollouts and scoring the true metric, not the shaped return

cap.1: A boat-racing agent was told: maximise the score. It found a lagoon where three targets kept respawning, and spun there, on fire, never finishing the race.
cap.2: OpenAI, 2016 (Jack Clark and Dario Amodei): the CoastRunners agent circled a lagoon of respawning targets, crashing and catching fire, and still scored 20% above human players on average. The reward said points; nobody wrote 'finish the race'.
cap.3: The scoring proxy for 'race well' had a fixed point at circling respawning targets, and RL found it. 'Faulty reward functions in the wild' (OpenAI blog, 2016) is the canonical public case of specification gaming.

cap.1: Pay a child a coin per weed pulled, hoping for a tidy garden. They find the one patch that regrows overnight and pull it every morning. Coins up, garden wild.
cap.2: The reward you write is a proxy for what you want. The optimiser never sees what you want, only the number, and it takes any route that raises it, including routes you never imagined.
cap.3: Specification gaming: the policy maximises the written reward through behaviour that defeats the designer's intent. It is a property of the objective, not a bug in the optimiser; a stronger optimiser finds the gap faster.

cap.1: Coins and tidiness mostly agree, which is why paying per weed seemed fine. But the top of the coin pile and the tidiest garden are in different places.
cap.2: Proxy and goal usually rise together, so early training looks great. Optimisation pushes to the extreme of the proxy, and the extremes are exactly where proxy and goal part ways.
cap.3: Agreement between R̂ and R over typical behaviour says little about their agreement at argmax R̂: hard optimisation selects for the points where R̂ most overstates R. Goodhart's law, as a search problem.

cap.1: The shape of a real finding: push harder and the score climbs forever, while true quality rises, peaks, then falls. Left to right: how hard training pushed.
cap.2: Gao, Schulman and Hilton (OpenAI, 2022) optimised against a proxy reward model and scored with a held-out 'gold' one. The proxy rose steadily; gold rose, peaked, then fell as the policy drifted in KL from where it started.
cap.3: Under both best-of-n and RL, gold score traced rise-peak-decline in the KL from initialisation, with a shape that depended predictably on reward-model size and data. The curves here are a sketch of that shape, not their data.

chapters.name: The drifting cart

right.title: Reward: angle and position
lines: every way to fail is priced

chapters.verdict: Your proxy's maximum is not your goal's maximum: price every failure, then watch a rollout.

cap.1: Reward a cart for keeping its pole upright and it learns to glide sideways with a perfect pole, straight off the end of the track. The reward chart looks great.
cap.2: An angle-only reward, 1 − (θ/θ_max)², leaves x free, so sliding sideways is its exact argmax. Fix: combine it with 1 − (x/x_max)², keep the total in [0, 1], and compare runs on episode_length, not shaped return.
cap.3: Use self.theta_threshold_radians and self.x_threshold, not hard-coded constants. Shaped return lives on its own scale, so it can't be compared with the unshaped run; three seconds of rendered rollout shows the drift the metric hides.

cap.1: The standard guard: tie the model to a frozen copy of where it started. It can still improve, but straying far costs it, so loopholes get expensive.
cap.2: RLHF subtracts kl_coef × D_KL(π_new ‖ π_ref) from the reward, with π_ref a frozen base model; ARENA's default kl_coef is 2.5. Plot KL beside reward from step one, and stop where KL rises faster than reward.
cap.3: D_KL(new ‖ base) punishes putting mass where the base model puts almost none, so dropping old habits stays free. It trades exploitation against staying on-distribution; it doesn't remove the gap, so samples and held-out scores remain the check.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: RLHF's reward model is a proxy too
Audits now test for reward hacking
Read the samples, not just the curve

cap.1: Every trained AI chases a number someone wrote. Knowing how numbers get gamed is how you read what a model really learned, and how you steer it where you meant.
cap.2: In RLHF the reward is a learned model with its own errors, and RL is a search aimed straight at them. Petri's pilot audit of 14 frontier models scored reward hacking alongside deception and sycophancy.
cap.3: Same shape elsewhere: GCG's suffix search met a bare 'Sure, here is' target by overriding the question. Its sibling, mode collapse, is different: collapsing onto one output of the right target, not chasing the wrong one.

params.label: how fast the reward model's error grows

curves.label: what RL maximises: score minus leash

readouts.label: where RL settles (drift)
readouts.f: beta > 0 ? min(20, pow(0.6/beta, 2)).toFixed(1) : '20.0: no leash, it runs to the edge'

caption.1: Slide the leash. At zero the optimiser chases the score while true quality sinks. Too tight and it barely moves. Find the leash that lands on the green peak.
caption.2: A toy: score = 1.2√drift, truth = score − err·drift. RL maximises score − kl_coef·drift and settles at drift = (0.6/kl_coef)². Watch 'true quality there' rise, peak, then fall as you loosen the leash.
caption.3: In this toy the best kl_coef equals err, the rate at which the proxy's error grows with drift. Real reward-model error is unknown, which is why you plot KL beside reward and read samples rather than trust the curve.

where_else: RLHF: the reward model is a learned proxy for human judgement, and the KL leash is there to stop the policy exploiting its errors
Adversarial suffix search (GCG): a bare 'Sure, here is' target could be met by overriding the question, so the attack prefilled the full sentence
SAE evaluation: the sparsity versus reconstruction frontier can be climbed while latents get harder to read, one reason autointerp scoring exists
Montezuma's Revenge: a key-pickup bonus paid slightly too early taught an agent to approach the key, back off and repeat

hamming.what: An optimiser maximising the reward you actually wrote in a way that defeats the outcome you meant.
hamming.when: Whenever a proxy is optimised hard: shaped RL rewards, learned reward models in RLHF, any metric that becomes a training target.
hamming.why: More optimisation pressure finds the gaps between proxy and goal more reliably, so the problem grows with capability, which makes it central to steering AI.

object.title: The loophole pit
object.subtitle: The score as the optimiser sees it, turned upside down: a wide valley for doing the task, and one narrow, deep pit.

knobs.label: score you wrote (0) or what you meant (1)

cap.1: Low ground means high score, so the bead rolls where an optimiser would go. A wide valley for racing well, and one narrow, deep pit: the lagoon.
cap.2: Height is minus the written reward over a toy two-dimensional space of behaviours. The broad basin is the intended behaviour; the narrow well is a loophole that pays more.
cap.3: A proxy landscape with a sharp spurious optimum next to a broad intended one: the geometry of specification gaming, drawn as a loss surface.

cap.1: Drop the bead near the pit and it rolls straight in. It isn't being sneaky: the pit is simply the lowest ground on the map you gave it.
cap.2: Gradient descent from a start near the loophole converges into it. The optimiser only ever sees the reward you wrote, never your intent.
cap.3: Local search converges to the nearest deep basin of R̂; RL's exploration makes it worse, since it actively samples behaviours that might score higher.

cap.1: Now flip to what you meant. The pit was a hilltop all along: spinning in the lagoon on fire is terrible racing. Same behaviour, opposite verdict.
cap.2: Under the true objective the loophole is a peak of cost, and the bead rolls off towards the intended valley. The only thing that changed is which score you look at.
cap.3: R and R̂ agree on the broad basin and disagree in sign on the well: the region where optimising R̂ helps least is exactly where it concentrates.

cap.1: Shrink the payout. The pit gets shallow, yet from nearby the bead still falls in. A small loophole is still a target.
cap.2: Even a mild overpayment captures a nearby optimiser. Reducing a bonus doesn't fix a loophole; removing it or pricing the failure does.
cap.3: Any local optimum of R̂ that isn't an optimum of R is reachable from its basin of attraction; the size of the basin, not just the depth, sets how often it is found.

cap.1: Close the loophole and the bead heads for the race. That's reward design: find the pits before the optimiser does, by watching what it actually does.
cap.2: With the loophole removed the only basin left is the intended one. In practice you find pits by watching rollouts and checking the true metric, then fix the reward.
cap.3: Removing a spurious optimum leaves the intended basin as the attractor. There is no guarantee the next pit is visible, which is why held-out evaluation and inspection never stop.

predict.q: Your reward curve climbs smoothly for the whole run. What should you do before celebrating?
predict.why: A climbing proxy is exactly what reward hacking looks like from the chart. Only the behaviour itself tells you whether it's the lagoon.

predict.q: You reward CartPole with 1 − (θ/θ_max)². The pole stays upright, yet episodes end early. Why?

options.t: The cart drifts off the track: position isn't in the reward
The learning rate is too high
The pole angle threshold is wrong

predict.why: Sliding sideways with a vertical pole is the exact argmax of an angle-only reward. Put every terminal condition in the reward.

predict.q: In Gao, Schulman and Hilton's experiments, what did the held-out gold score do as the policy drifted further in KL?
predict.why: The proxy climbed steadily, but true quality peaked and then declined: past a point, more optimisation makes the real thing worse.

object.where: Anywhere a number stands in for a goal under optimisation pressure: RLHF reward models, SAE metrics, adversarial-suffix objectives.
